newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Don't look for science in latest dino blockbuster.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Don't look for science in latest dino blockbuster.

text.p: The dinosaurs look good and sound good, and they are piling adults and kids alike into cinemas, but the scientific adviser to Stephen Spielberg's latest blockbuster "The Lost World" says it's all fiction.
John Horner, the Montana dinosaur hunter who helped inspire the lead character in Spielberg's entertaining but fictional "Jurassic Park," says there is even less truth in the sequel.
"There's hardly any science in it at all," Horner said in an interview during a promotional tour of Britain. "This is just a scary movie."
The dinosaurs depicted in "The Lost World" do not act like any animal that ever walked the Earth, and it would be impossible to clone a dinosaur anyway, Horner said.

So much for the premise of both films, and the books by Michael on -- that a wealthy entrepreneur hired scientists to clone dinosaurs from DNA, and that the resulting creatures rampaged through their theme park home, tearing open cars, trailers and buildings to get at the people inside.
CLONING DLOUS"
Horner -- who has himself found what may be dinosaur DNA -- says the whole idea is ridiculous.
"We can't make dinosaurs -- we can't clone anything from DNA," he said.

Anyway, for trying to clone an animal "DNA is actually pretty useless." The entire DNA inventory of an animal is unbelievably enormous, with hundreds of thousands of genes. One fragment of DNA would not be enough to code for even one gene, let alone a whole animal.
Horner's team did recover bits of DNA from a dinosaur fossil, but it did not contain much useful information.
He said it was entirely likely the DNA he recovered was that of ancient bacteria.
"When an animal begins to deteriorate it literally is covered with bacteria. That bacteria covering it is what's preserved."
As for the film's original premise -- that dinosaur DNA was pulled from the bodies of ancient bloodsucking insects preserved in amber -- Horner snorts derisively.
Even if it was possible to get DNA, it would be a huge step to clone an actual animal, said Horner, who works at the Museum of the Rockies at Montana State University.
He said to clone a dinosaur you would first have to get a dinosaur cell or a dinosaur egg. Getting a live dinosaur cell is impossible.
Eggs can be cloned and dinosaur eggs have been found, but they are fossilised -- turned virtually to stone.
Horner said the films ignore such difficult facts, and he saw no point in pressing the issue. "I would have just said 'no, you can't do it' and they wouldn't have had their movie," he said.
CAR CHASES MAY BE FUN, BUT NOT FOR T REX
Horner also complains about the way the dinosaurs act in the movies -- chasing cars, tearing open trailers in furious revenge and pursuing their human captors.
"Animals don't get even. Animals aren't mean," Horner said. "We can study tigers. We can study lions. They don't eat us for fun."
"Animals are territorial but we can walk into their territory without being eaten or without our car being eaten."
Horner reminds those who have not kept up with the latest dinosaur news that scientists now do not believe one of the show's stars, the Tyrannosaurus rex, was a vicious predator.
"A predatory animal needs to be able to grab hold of things," Horner said. Tyrannosaurs had tiny little arms and huge, lumbering legs.
"It didn't run fast. T rex was a slow animal."

Its skull also shows a huge olfactory lobe -- meaning it had a very keen sense of smell. "Animals that can smell long-distance are things like turkey vultures -- animals that eat dead things," he said. "Tyrannosaurus rex was probably a scavenger."
Another small error -- the stars of the films, the velociraptors, were actually modelled on another kind of dinosaur known as deinonychus.
But Crichton preferred the name velociraptor. "So you could say this is deinonychus but its stage name is velociraptor."
There is, however, a little bit of good science, Horner concedes. "Fact and fiction are woven together," he said.
BUT VELOCIRAPTORS REALLY WERE SCARY
The velociraptors are one group of dinosaurs in the movies that way the real animals would have.
As in the film, they had sickle-shaped claws and a fossil found in Mongolia is clearly a deinonychus entangled with a triceratops. There is no doubt the meat-eater was disembowelling the triceratops.
"It's one of the most important fossils ever found, because it shows how the velociraptor killed its prey," Horner said.
Palaentologists think the two animals died together during a struggle when a sand dune collapsed on top of them 75 million years ago.

There is also evidence the deinonychus and velociraptors hunted in packs. Both lose their teeth easily and replace them through life much as a shark does, and fossil remains of kills have shown more teeth than would fit in one animal's mouth, Horner says.
He admits he sometimes gets annoyed when people believe fiction is true. "It is frustrating," he said.
Sometimes, he said, "you just have to bite your tongue."
But the movies do some good. "It's a double-edged sword," he said. "I'm trying to keep the interest in science up and not let the fiction run away."
Children are definitely interested in dinosaurs. "But it takes something like 'The Lost World' to get adults interested in them," he said. "It draws them in."
And Horner sees no problem with a professional palaeontologist promoting a movie. "Our job is not to sit in the office all the time and work on scientific papers so other scientists can read them."
He also confesses to using the film for his own personal ends. One of the characters in the film resembles a palaeontologist rival, and spouts theories that Horner has questioned for years.
"So Stephen Spielberg and I, we just had to have this guy eaten," Horner laughs.
